# Denominator sweep — missing features not yet in the capability ledger

Produced by the ledger-closure denominator sweep over the two coverage maps, at repo
`/Users/i.i.gavrikov/Desktop/work/nessy-desktop`, branch `feat/TCODE-000`, HEAD `34be43fde`, tree clean.
Every row below is a capability the two maps carry that the capability ledger
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-28-capability-ledger.md` does **not** have a row for. Classification
vocabulary (`CLOSED_AT_HEAD` / `BUILDABLE` / `OWNER` / `STRUCTURAL` / `MEASURE`, sizes `S`/`M`/`L`) and the
evidence tiers are the closure brief's; each row cites at least one `file:line`, commit, or page anchor.

**The VERDICT vocabulary of the Pi/Claude/Codex columns is this file's own, and it is MARKER-LESS: `have`,
`partial`, `absent`, `n/a`, `unknown` — five words, no provenance marker.** It is not the capability
ledger's, whose first word is `covered` and whose cells carry one of five markers; when an edit there is
mirrored here, `covered` becomes `have` (the mapping is stated in the QM5 apply readme). C3.320 swept the
last fifteen cells that still read `covered` — A80, F26, G25, J27, K31 and G11 ×3 in the Claude column,
H28, H46 and L35's Pi cell in Pi, K10, L22 and L35's other two in Codex — 2026-09-12. Backticking is
inconsistent across rows (about half of the 1 575 verdict cells wear backticks) and is deliberately left
as each row wrote it. Until 2026-09-12 the argument for that rested on **"no script parses these columns
at all"** — `scripts/plan-status.py` reads the capability ledger and not this file, and
`scripts/check-ledger-citations.ts` reads this file for its CITATIONS rather than its verdicts. C3.341
made that sentence false: `scripts/check-denominator-twin.ts` (`lint:denominator-twin`, a step of
`lint:chain`) now counts this table's twelve fields and reads exactly these three columns. It does not
weaken the rule, it enforces it — `verdictWord` strips the backticks off either side and compares THE
WORD, so both spellings are the same verdict to the only reader there is. Normalising the typography
would still bury the one kind of change that carries meaning. The word is the contract; the backticks
are not.

Corroborating glyph counts at HEAD: the Claude map carries 204 🟨 and 82 🟥 cells (against 232 🟩 and 237 ⬜);
the codex map carries 82 🟨 and 23 🟥 (against 9 🟩 and 5 ⬜). A page/row carries several cells, so the glyph
totals are larger than the page/row denominators above and are not a second count of the same thing.

## What was NOT swept, and why that is acceptable — and where it is not

**The 🟩 pages and rows were not swept.** A 🟩 cell is a page whose capability the maps record as already
covered, and the sweep's question is "what is missing that the ledger has no row for". Re-reading a page the
map calls covered would re-derive rows the ledger already carries. This is acceptable **only to the strength of
the map's own marker** — and that is exactly where it is not acceptable: a 🟩 set by a `ˢ` (propagated) or `ᵈ`
(doc-only) marker is a claim, not a measurement, and the same map records 23 pages it calls 🟩 that the parity
report calls "cited by nobody" (`2026-07-31-claude-coverage-map.md:55` — "the only real contradiction"). **Those
23 are an unswept residue with a known name, and they are the first place a missing row will be found.**

**The ⬜ pages and rows were not swept.** ⬜ is out-of-corpus or not-applicable — 237 cells on the Claude map,
5 on the codex map. This is acceptable because the ⬜ marker is itself a scope ruling already made, and the
map's own reconciliation table (`:53`) records that the report and the map "were never counting the same set".
Where it is **not** acceptable: ⬜ was in several places set for a *contingent* reason (no WSL launcher exists,
no Cloud mode exists), and a contingent exclusion silently becomes a gap the day the precondition is built.
Those are recorded under **Out of scope** below rather than dropped, precisely so the honest-surface obligation
survives — see D's WSL row and I's Cloud-mode row.

**Nothing else was dropped.** 0 enumerate/refute slices were dropped (none). 0 reduce chunks were dropped
(none). 0 groups were dropped (none) — all fifteen groups A–O produced a section file and all fifteen are
concatenated below verbatim.

## How this file was built

The fifteen per-group section files under `work/denominator-gaps/` were concatenated by shell (`awk` between the
`#### In scope` and `#### Out of scope` markers); **no row was retyped**. The in-scope row count was then verified
with `grep -c` against the sum of the fifteen groups' own counts: **525 = 525**.

Four reasons, and each one is a decision this host can defend: (1) **the destination has no reader**, so a persisted write would be a rule that silently does nothing — `setMode` anywhere but `session` (*"permissions.defaultMode has no reader"*), `addDirectories` (*"permissions.additionalDirectories has no reader"*), and any destination with no reader at all; (2) **it would edit a file this session did not author** — `removeRules` and `removeDirectories` at a persisted destination, *"including an administrator's"*, and a configured root is not hook-removable; (3) **it would widen the floor past what the prompt offered** — `bypassPermissions` is refused unless the session is already there, *"never hook-widened, never persisted"*, a persistent allow is accepted only when it echoes a `permission_suggestion` this prompt offered, and a Bash rule resolving to a dangerous or empty base command is never session-whitelisted; (4) **it is not enforceable or not recognised** — an unparseable rule, an unrecognised mode, an unknown entry type. Every one of the twenty-one is delivered through the same `__PERMISSION_UPDATE__` debug record the applied set uses, so a hook author gets the reason rather than silence, which is the whole difference between this being a decision and being a gap. **macOS: the three runtimes do not say the same thing about an approved Bash command, and the
difference is not two-way** (C3.130, 2026-09-11 — the non-skippable half of that row, written here
because until now this fact existed only inside the owner-sitting page, and an unstated boundary
difference is the silent-divergence shape this fork's largest defect class is made of). There are
THREE darwin containment surfaces, not one.

1. The per-command Bash seatbelt on Pi — `packages/shared/src/agent/core/bash-seatbelt.ts` — ships
   `SEATBELT_TESTING_WILDCARD: boolean = true`, so the profile it emits is `(version 1) (allow
   default)`: an approved Bash command is NOT contained. The strict profile it replaces
   (`packages/shared/src/agent/core/bash-seatbelt.ts` symbol `buildStrictMacosBashSeatbeltProfile`,
   `(deny default)`) is built, exercised by the suite, and held open only by that constant.
2. The supervised-process isolation profile — `packages/session-tools-core/src/runtime/filesystem-isolation.ts`
   symbol `buildDarwinSandboxProfile`, used by `packages/server-core/src/pi-harness/isolation/darwin.ts`
   — carries NO wildcard and binds what it is given.
3. codex's own sandbox emits `(deny default)`, natively, with nothing of ours in the path.

Above all three sits the standing decision that isolation is OFF by default (2026-08-12/13, owner
sitting §1.1 of 2026-09-05, reaffirmed by the owner's answer to QI5 of 2026-09-11), so on a shipped
default the boundary is not engaged on Pi at all — which is why §1.1's own title is that an approved
Bash command is uncontained, and why no cell in this cluster reads `have`. The residue is the host's
to make uniform or honest; today it is honest here and nowhere else.

**The flat version of this sentence is refused on purpose.** Saying only that *an approved Bash
command IS contained on codex and is NOT on Pi* is true of ONE of the three surfaces above, and
`bash-seatbelt.ts`'s own docblock says so in its own words: it would state a two-way difference where
the tree has a three-way one, which is the same shape of over-flat claim this whole exercise exists
to correct.

## Out of scope

### A. The safety floor — what stops a harmful action

| capability | source page(s) | reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grant workspace trust per distribution and folder, so a folder trusted in one distribution is not trusted in another or at the same path on Windows. | `desktop-wsl` | Contingent on a WSL session capability that does not exist at HEAD — no WSL launcher, so the extra trust dimension has nothing to protect; inherits P3.7's park. Mandatory the day a WSL launcher is built: a trust key without the distribution reuses one trust decision across two filesystems. Evidence: `packages/server-core/src/sessions/SessionManager.ts` symbol `projectTrustState`, :3013, :3053 (`projectTrustState === 'trusted'`); https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop-wsl.md#start-a-wsl-session |
| Run auto mode on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry, replacing prompts with background safety checks. | `whats-new/2026-w23` | Precondition refused by construction: all SEVEN `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_*` provider toggles are stripped from the claude child and the host env, so no session of ours can run on Bedrock, Agent Platform or Foundry. claude-provider-routing-env.ts:145-153 (`CLAUDE_PROVIDER_SELECTION_TOGGLE_ENV_KEYS`), folded into `CLAUDE_SDK_STRIPPED_ENV_KEYS` at :284-288, cleared in `packages/shared/src/agent/claude-agent.ts` symbol `postInit`, through `clearClaudeCloudProviderRoutingEnvVars`. The judge behind auto mode stays in A1; only the provider surface is out. Side finding: the ledger's C5 narrative ('we strip five, and the two we do not') is stale at HEAD. |
| Have `/commit-push-pr` auto-allow `git push` to the repo's configured push remote in addition to `origin`. | `whats-new/2026-w28` | A bundled CLI command we do not ship (`/commit-push-pr`); the underlying push-remote auto-allow rule has no host counterpart. ### B. What an organisation can actually enforce

## Per runtime

Of the **525 in-scope missing features**, how each runtime stands. The four buckets do not sum to 525 on any
runtime because a cell may be `n/a` — the runtime has no such surface, which is not a gap: 22 `n/a` on Pi,
17 on claude, 36 on codex.

| runtime | absent (lacks) | partial (lacks partly) | have | unknown | n/a | cells counted |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Pi** | **227** | 110 | 98 | 68 | 22 | 503 |
| **claude** | **233** | 117 | 86 | 72 | 17 | 508 |
| **codex** | **269** | 99 | 50 | 71 | 36 | 489 |

Per group, absent counts: Pi A31 B16 C8 D2 E2 F16 G5 H21 I15 J20 K11 L45 M21 N6 O8; claude A34 B17 C10 D3 E2
F19 G5 H22 I17 J21 K12 L42 M14 N6 O9; codex A36 B17 C9 D1 E2 F21 G6 H30 I18 J26 K13 L55 M20 N6 O9.

The shape is asymmetric and the asymmetry is not the one the totals suggest. **Codex is thinnest by a wide
margin** (269 absent, only 50 `have`) yet it is also where the *unused native mechanisms* are richest — granular
approval categories, per-server MCP approval modes, per-turn `sandboxPolicy`, named permission profiles,
`plan_mode_reasoning_effort`, `agents.default_subagent_model`, `service_tier`, `[agents] enabled` — all present
in its own schema and written by no host code. **claude carries the most `unknown` (72)** because the binary is
closed and several documented keys sit ahead of the vendored 2.1.233 bundle. **C3.252 2026-09-12 (W17-z), the version clause only:** the vendored bundle is `2.1.247`; several documented keys still sit ahead of it, but FEWER, and the ones this lane found to have been overtaken are corrected in their own cells. **Pi has the most `have` (98)**
because Pi is the runtime we build to the documentation ourselves.

### The four biggest themes across all fifteen groups

**1. A control that registers successfully and then never controls — this is the single largest and most
dangerous class, and it recurs in every group.** Workspace trust drops an untrusted repo's DENY and ASK rules
along with its allow rules (A15); a project file can still set `permissions.defaultMode` to `bypassPermissions`
(A16) and a session that ended in bypass reopens in it (A17); a claude-runtime session **discards the host's
entire managed slice** on any machine carrying a Claude Code admin source without `parentSettingsBehavior:
"merge"` (B9) and the win32 arm enforces nothing at all (B10); every allowlist we ship is advisory because its
exclusivity half is missing (`allowManagedMcpServersOnly`, B11); a WebFetch deny is not a network boundary (C6);
hooks' ConfigChange block is advisory where the page says the setting must not be applied, and `once: true`
burns on matcher *match* rather than on run success, so a policy hook that exits 2 retires itself (G); both
telemetry exporters treat any non-429/non-5xx collector response as success inside a bare `catch {}` (M); the
macOS seatbelt ships a testing wildcard and `sandbox.failIfUnavailable` has zero readers (I6, I11). In every
one of these the mechanism reports success and the enforcement is absent.

**2. The host already holds the fact and simply says nothing — a missing sentence, not a missing mechanism.**
This is the cheapest large block of value in the whole sweep. Nothing shows the user what policy is actually in
force, and the five surfaces that would (A42–A46) each read a data structure that already exists in one
function. `buildConfigDoctorReport` already names the winning managed source, shadowed sources and dropped
entries — and its only production consumer is `apps/cli/src/doctor.ts`, so a desktop user cannot diagnose a
settings, plugin or MCP misconfiguration at all (M). Claude's `modelUsage` is produced, persisted, telemetered
and read by zero renderer code; codex's `TokenUsageBreakdown` cache fields and its zero-caller
`GetAccountTokenUsage` RPC are computed upstream and reach no reader (M). A restore that leaves a bash-deleted
file deleted, a retry with no attempt counter, a worker shutting down mid-session, a codex child that dies
between spawn and initialize — nine new sites in group F alone (F). Our own privacy posture silently removes
four claude features on the gateway connection only, and the reason lives as a code comment (D5).

**3. Native-first was not asked, and the runtime's own mechanism is sitting unset.** Step 1 of the owner rule —
*does the runtime already have it* — is unanswered across a large block of rows.
`CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPLORE_PLAN_AGENTS`, `CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_DISABLE_BUILTIN_AGENTS`, `Query.backgroundTasks`,
`Options.taskBudget`, `enableWorkflows`/`workflowSizeGuideline` (H31, H32, H16, H47, H43, H45); claude's own
`reconnectMcpServer`/`toggleMcpServer`/`strictMcpConfig`/`enabledMcpjsonServers` (J); Claude's eight sandbox
network-transport keys, native in the vendored bundle and projected nowhere (C9); the SDK's `capabilities` array
published precisely so callers feature-detect, whose only reader is a test fixture (D7); `Query.getContextUsage()`
at `sdk.d.ts:2509` and `SDKAssistantMessage.context_usage` at `:3058`, called once and then amputated at
`applySdkContextUsage(usage: { model?, rawMaxTokens? })` so the categories cannot enter the host (E). And the
inverse: **bundle-lag runs both ways** — four documented keys score zero in the shipped SDK, so nothing native
can be enabled there and the host must build (K).

**4. The same exported name is honoured, ignored, or dead depending on which runtime the session is on — an
unannounced switch cost.** Operator ceilings are honoured on claude *by an accident* of the wholesale
`process.env` spread in `buildClaudeSubprocessEnv`, and by nothing else: the tool memory cap, Bash cwd
carry-over, `CLAUDE_CODE_GLOB_NO_IGNORE`, `defaultShell`, PowerShell, `USE_BUILTIN_RIPGREP` all reach the
vendored binary while Pi and codex read none of them (J). Five model/cache environment names ride the same
accident (K). What steers the model diverges three ways with no diagnostic naming it — subdirectory
`CLAUDE.md`, `paths:`-scoped `.claude/rules/`, the ancestor chain, additional-directory instruction loading, and
codex's silent 32 KiB truncation of the instruction chain (L). Subagent frontmatter crosses to the Claude SDK
verbatim at `claude-runtime-agents.ts:845-850` and is dropped by codex at `packages/codex-responses-adapter/src/config-writer.ts` symbol `sanitizeCodexRoleName` **with no
diagnostic** (H). This is native-first's second half going unpaid: the residual difference is neither uniform
nor honest.

*A fifth, structural, worth naming because it changes what "closing" costs:* several of the largest-looking
clusters are **one host build serving all three runtimes**, not three ports. Plugins and marketplaces (L74–L116)
are host construction because the host passes `plugins: []` and projects every component itself. The whole of
group N funnels through one choke point (`cross-session-inbound.ts` + `admitAgentMessage`), which is why its
three runtime columns move together. 13 of O's 15 rows are one Electron renderer or one main-process seam. Six
of F's proposed rows inherit F1's single producer gap. The review loop — line-anchored diff comments,
`/simplify`, a backgrounded `/code-review`, a sticky effort level, `/security-review` — is absent identically on
all three (H14–H18), so it is host-seam work and no kind of switch divergence.

## What this changes about the parity figure

The capability ledger's denominator is **107** capabilities. This sweep adds **N = 525** in-scope capabilities
the ledger has no row for. The denominator therefore grows from **107 to 632**.

**No percentage is recomputed here, deliberately.** The ledger's current headline — 92 of 107 not `covered` on
every runtime, Pi 63 %, Claude 44 %, Codex 36 %, Host 52 % — is scored by `scripts/plan-status.py` (line ~96)
from the ledger's own `Switch` column. These 525 rows are not ledger rows: they carry no `Switch` verdict and no
ledger marker, so any percentage mixing the two sets would be counting two different things, which is the exact
error the coverage-map reconciliation table already records once (`2026-07-31-claude-coverage-map.md:53` — the
report and the map "were never counting the same set"). The figure moves when these rows are **admitted** to the
ledger with verdicts, not when they are counted.

What can be stated without recomputation:

| | value |
| --- | --- |
| ledger denominator today | 107 |
| **N — in-scope capabilities added by this sweep** | **525** |
| ledger denominator after admission | 632 |
| out-of-scope entries recorded (classified, not added) | 124 |
| **Pi — absent** | **227** |
| **claude — absent** | **233** |
| **codex — absent** | **269** |

The absent counts above are the strict `absent` bucket only. Adding `partial` — a cell that lacks the capability
in part — gives 337 for Pi, 350 for claude and 368 for codex, and adding `unknown` (never measured on that
runtime) gives 405 / 422 / 439. Which of those three is the honest numerator is itself a decision the ledger's
own vocabulary already makes: `—` and `ˢ`/`ᵏ` markers are claims, not measurements.

Two consequences worth putting in front of the owner before any lane is dispatched:

1. **The sweep found roughly five times more missing capability than the ledger tracks.** A parity figure quoted
   against 107 is not wrong, but it is a figure about the ledger, not about the product. Any external statement
   of "parity" should name its denominator.
2. **The count is not the cost.** A large fraction of the 525 is one host build serving all three runtimes
   (plugins/marketplaces, cross-session messaging, notifications/UI, the review loop, checkpoint producers), and
   another large fraction is a *sentence* the host already has the data for. The rows that are genuinely
   expensive are far fewer than 525, and the rows that need an owner posture before any code — telemetry
   personal data, export content volume, egress, containerised execution, the price table — are fewer still.
